paper_a.title: Universal Approximation Theorem for a Single-Layer Transformer

paper_b.title: A unified framework for establishing the universal approximation of transformer-type architectures

metadata.description: Both papers establish that transformer-type architectures are universal approximators of continuous sequence-to-sequence functions on compact domains. Paper A gives a direct constructive proof for a single multi-head attention + FFN block via Heine-Cantor partitioning and Hahn-Banach indicator separation. Paper B abstracts the same conclusion into a general framework whose hypotheses (nonlinear/affine-invariant FFN family plus token-distinguishability of the mixing family) imply UAP for many concrete attention variants (kernel, sparse, LinFormer, SkyFormer, bias-term). The relationship is best classified as an alternative proof: same UAP target, fundamentally different proof technique (constructive head-per-region vs. interpolation + tensor-type approximation reduction).

matches.explanation: TP468.4 is the single-layer transformer UAP: any continuous f on compact X is approximated to arbitrary epsilon by one MHA + FFN block. TP465.1 is the abstract framework theorem giving G-UAP for any T_{G,H} satisfying nonlinearity/affine-invariance and token distinguishability; CP465.1 is its specialization to standard kernel attention which, like TP468.4, also achieves UAP with a single token-mixing layer plus enough feedforward layers. The conclusions match (universal approximation of continuous functions on compact domains by transformer architectures with sufficient width), but Paper B's statement is more general (arbitrary symmetry group G, arbitrary nonlinear FFN family, arbitrary token-mixing satisfying an abstract condition), while Paper A is the concrete softmax case. Tagged analogous because the precise functional class (G-equivariant L^p approximation vs sup-norm continuous approximation) and hypotheses differ even though the underlying claim is the same.

Composite many-to-many alignment of the proofs of the main UAP theorems. Both proofs are constructive and discretize the compact domain, but the assembly differs fundamentally. Paper A's proof PP468.1 partitions X via Heine-Cantor (PSP468.1), picks region representatives (PSP468.2), assigns one attention head per region (PSP468.3), separates regions via Hahn-Banach (PSP468.4), uses softmax sharpening to concentrate attention (PSP468.5), aggregates heads via output projection (PSP468.6), uses FFN as identity (PSP468.7), and bounds total error (PSP468.8). Paper B's proof PP465.1 instead reduces UAP to two intermediate building blocks: an interpolation property PrP465.1 (delivered via PrP465.3 / Cheng-Lin-Shen-Li 2025 ResNet interpolation) and a tensor-type approximation PrP465.2; then on a discretization grid (PSP465.1) it applies interpolation pointwise (PSP465.2), approximates a contracting tensor map (PSP465.3) and bounds composition error (PSP465.4). Both yield epsilon-approximation but the techniques are disjoint: head-per-region softmax-sharpening vs. interpolation-on-grid + contracting-map approximation. This is the heart of the AP classification. Composite L2 entry per the v2 prompt rule for L1 parents whose inner step DAGs differ in interesting ways.

Both define the same scaled-dot-product self-attention mechanism. Paper A's DP468.4 introduces queries/keys/values q_i = x_i W^Q, k_i = x_i W^K, v_i = x_i W^V and z_i = sum_j alpha_{ij} v_j; Paper B's EP465.2 writes the same operation summed over heads as W_V X softmax((W_K X)^T W_Q X). Same mathematical object.

Scaled-dot-product softmax attention weights and their matrix form (alpha_{ij} = exp((q_i.k_j)/sqrt(d)) / Z; Z = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d)) V) match the softmax expression inside Paper B's EP465.2. Notation differs but the operation is identical.

Paper A's DP468.6 is the multi-head attention concatenation MHA(X) = Concat(Z_1,...,Z_h)W^O; Paper B's EP465.2 instead writes multi-head attention as a sum over heads sum_i W_V^{t,i} X softmax(...). Concat-then-project and sum-over-heads with per-head W_V are equivalent up to absorbing W^O into the W_V's, but the surface form differs. Medium confidence because the equivalence is standard but never made explicit in either JSON.

Paper A's DP468.7 defines a single Transformer block as MHA + position-wise FFN with skip connections. Paper B's DP465.1 defines a transformer block as (Id + h) o (Id + g) with g token-mixing and h token-wise; EP465.1 spells out the two-step residual update X_{t+1/2} = X_t + Atten(X_t), X_{t+1} = X_{t+1/2} + FFN(X_{t+1/2}). Identical architectural definition with explicit residual / Pre-Norm formulation in B.

Both characterize positional encoding as fixed/learned vectors added to tokens to break the permutation invariance of attention. Paper B's RP465.1 additionally formalizes its role as the bridge from G-UAP to general (non-equivariant) UAP, but the underlying object is the same.

Paper A cites the classical Cybenko/Hornik UAP for one-hidden-layer feedforward networks. Paper B cites the Cheng-Lin-Shen-Li 2025 universal interpolation / approximation theorem for Lipschitz residual networks (Id+H)^*. Both serve the same role in their respective proofs: a feedforward UAP/interpolation primitive that the transformer UAP construction reduces to. Different theorems (shallow MLP UAP vs deep ResNet interpolation) but analogous role; both are cited external building blocks.

Paper A cites Heine-Cantor (TP468.2) explicitly to obtain a finite epsilon-partition of the compact domain in PSP468.1. Paper B does the same step implicitly inside PSP465.1 (piecewise-constant approximation by uniform continuity of F on K), without naming the theorem. Same analytic ingredient, different surface form.

Paper A invokes Hahn-Banach separation (TP468.3) in PSP468.4 to construct linear functionals that distinguish regions. Paper B's framework does not need a separation theorem: indicator-region geometry is replaced by the interpolation property of (Id+H)^* (PrP465.3) and by the abstract token-distinguishability hypothesis on G. No counterpart in Paper B's proof machinery.

Paper A's gradient-descent update rule and SGD algorithm (background optimization material from a tutorial-style section) have no counterpart in Paper B, which is purely a representational/approximation-theoretic paper and never discusses training dynamics.
Paper A's backpropagation recursion, parameter-gradient formulas and the backprop algorithm itself are tutorial content from the optimization background; Paper B does not address training algorithms.
Adam optimizer is background material in Paper A with no counterpart in Paper B.

Paper A's foundational definitions (fully connected layer output, expected loss objective, cross-entropy loss) are introductory background. Paper B's framework operates at the architectural level of token-mixing g and token-wise h families and does not introduce these basic objects.

Paper B's central contribution of working modulo a permutation subgroup G (G-equivariance and G-UAP) is absent in Paper A, which only handles plain continuous functions on compact X without symmetry considerations. This is one of the main generalization axes of B over A.

The abstract nonlinearity + affine-invariance hypothesis on the FFN family H is the key abstraction that lets Paper B's framework cover many architectures uniformly. Paper A fixes the FFN to position-wise ReLU and does not isolate this condition.

Token-distinguishability (DP465.5) and its analytic two-sample reduction (TP465.2 + proof PP465.2) are Paper B's main conceptual tool for transferring UAP across attention variants. Paper A's construction (one head per region) is a direct ad-hoc replacement for distinguishability and never abstracts it; no counterpart.

Sparse attention machinery: sparsity-pattern adjacency and automorphism (DP465.6), the sparse transformer family T^Phi_H (DP465.7), connectivity within m layers (DP465.8), the sparse-attention UAP corollary (CP465.2) and its proof (PP465.4 + steps) are all Paper B contributions with no analogue in Paper A's dense single-layer setting.

Application of the framework to LinFormer / SkyFormer (CP465.3 corollary, EP465.4 LinFormer attention, EP465.5 SkyFormer kernelized attention, LP465.3 LinFormer equality lemma) — efficient-attention variants not addressed in Paper A.
New bias-term attention mechanism (EP465.6), its sparse UAP corollary (CP465.4) and proof (PP465.5) are novel contributions of Paper B with no counterpart in A.

D_n / C_n symmetric architectures (CP465.5), circular column-wise convolution (EP465.7) and the proof of automorphism = D_n for cyclic-window patterns (PP465.6) are equivariance applications absent from Paper A.

The kernel-based attention equation EP465.3, the kernel equality-of-attention lemma LP465.1, its scaling-limit auxiliary LP465.2, and the proof of CP465.1 (PP465.3) are technical machinery proper to Paper B's kernel-attention argument. Paper A only treats the standard softmax-dot-product kernel and does not consider the abstract-kernel generalization, so there is no counterpart.

Paper A's remark connecting its construction to the Deep Sets framework has no direct analogue in Paper B. Paper B's discussion of equivariance via G-UAP is much more general but never invokes Deep Sets explicitly.

Paper A's remark on capacity / latent-dimension lower bounds (Wagstaff et al.) has no counterpart in Paper B, which does not address quantitative width lower bounds (and explicitly notes in RP465.3 that quantitative rates are out of scope).

Both papers acknowledge the existence-vs-trainability / qualitative-vs-quantitative gap in their concluding remarks. Paper A's RP468.3 notes that TP468.4 is an existence result and gradient training may not recover the constructed parameters; Paper B's RP465.3 lists limitations including the lack of quantitative rates separating contributions of architecture components. Same flavor of caveat (non-constructive in the training sense) attached to similar UAP existence claims.
Paper A's distillation remark (deep transformer can be distilled into one wide layer) has no analogue in Paper B.
